sections.html:
Fauquier is a Northern Virginia county of about 651 square miles, mostly open Piedmont land, with Warrenton as its seat. Remington and The Plains are the other towns. The 2020 census counted 72,972 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 76,503. Exurban development from the Washington area has reached parts of the county, including housing along highways in rural areas.

Beyond the towns, many addresses and deeds use unincorporated names such as Bealeton, Calverton, Catlett, Marshall, Midland, New Baltimore, Opal, Paris, Rectortown and Upperville. New Baltimore is the largest community, and the Brookside and Vint Hill subdivisions feed growth in the east. Because 57.5 percent of residents lived in rural areas in 2020, land use rules come up more here than in a city.

Many owners use a Fauquier house as a base for a commute. Fauquier County Public Schools serves most of the county, and the part on Marine Corps Base Quantico belongs to the Defense Department's school system.

The Commissioner of the Revenue's rate page shows a combined real estate rate of $0.895 per $100 of assessed value. That figure is $0.709 base, $0.182 for the fire and rescue levy and $0.004 for the conservation easement fund.

One special district adds to the bill: the Marshall Electric Light and Business Improvement district adds $0.025 per $100. Mobile homes are taxed at the same $0.895 as real estate. Confirm the current-year figure with the office when you plan a sale.

The bill comes in two halves, one in June and one in December. Pay the Treasurer's Office, using the county's online tax portal for payments and balances. A date on a weekend moves to the next business day.

DateWhat is due
March 5Renewal for tax relief for the elderly, filed with the Commissioner of the Revenue
June 5First half real estate taxes
October 25Revalidation and new land use applications
December 5Second half real estate taxes

Before letting any bill slide, call the Treasurer's Office for the current penalty and interest.

Fauquier reassesses every four years. The last reassessment took effect January 1, 2026, the process carries through 2027, and new values take effect January 1, 2028.

The county's Board of Equalization hears property assessment disputes. The Circuit Court appoints its five members, who must be county residents and a majority freeholders, with at least 30 percent drawn from appraisal, real estate, building, legal or financial work. The deadline to appeal is set by ordinance, so ask the Commissioner's office for the date.

The Commissioner of the Revenue's office is at 10 Courthouse Square, 2nd Floor, Warrenton, VA 20186, phone (540) 422-8880. If the board's result is not enough, you can apply to the circuit court. Virginia Code 58.1-3984 presumes the assessor's value, or the board's adjusted value, is correct and puts the burden on the taxpayer to show the value was wrong and not set under accepted appraisal practice.

sections.h2: Timing a sale around the four-year cycle
sections.html:
Because Fauquier reassesses only every four years, your assessed value stays fixed for a long stretch while the market moves. The 2026 values will stand until the January 1, 2028 values take effect. If prices have climbed since the last reassessment, a buyer may be getting a tax figure that is low compared with a future bill. If prices have slipped, the reverse can be true.

Either way, be ready to explain the number. Give the buyer your assessment, the combined rate of $0.895 per $100, and the date the next values take effect, so they can plan for a change in the bill.

sections.h2: Preparing for a Board of Equalization hearing
sections.html:
The board is made up of county residents, many of them with an appraisal, real estate, building, legal or financial background, so a clear, factual case works better than frustration over a bill. State what you believe the value should be and why. Bring recent sales of similar houses, photos of any defects and repair estimates. Be ready for the board to start from the assumption that the assessor is right, which is the standard the court uses as well.

If the result is not enough, the next step is the circuit court. Ask the Commissioner's office about the deadline early, since it is set by ordinance and is not repeated on your bill.

The county's use value program taxes qualifying farm, forest, horticultural and open space land by its use, not its market value. If the land stops qualifying, a roll-back assessment applies, and the county requires repayment of the deferred tax plus 10 percent interest for five years plus the current year.

When you sell acreage, ask the Commissioner of the Revenue whether the parcel is in land use before you agree to a closing date, since a change in use can trigger the bill.

The county also offers real estate tax relief for owners age 65 and older or permanently disabled, with reduction or exemption based on income and net worth, applied for each year. The office number for that program is 540-422-8140.

For a Virginia house, the tax lien stands ahead of the others until it is paid off. Virginia Code 58.1-3340 sends sale proceeds first to taxes and levies on the real estate, with penalties and interest, and leaves the seller's share of the year to the contract.

Recording the deed costs the seller too. The grantor's tax is 50 cents per $500 under Virginia Code 58.1-802, unless the buyer agrees to take it on. Ownership records at the Commissioner's office are updated from deed transfers and other Clerk of the Circuit Court records, so a deed recorded late can mean the wrong person gets billed.

In practice: confirm what is paid with the Treasurer, add up any roll-back that a land use change would trigger, and put both numbers in front of your closing agent a week before the closing date. Ask for the final figures in writing and keep the receipts with your sale papers.

Ask the Treasurer which half is paid. Ask the Commissioner of the Revenue whether the land is enrolled in use value and whether relief applies. Decide whether to list now or after the January 1, 2028 values take effect, and look at your current assessment next to what a buyer is likely to pay. Make sure the deed is recorded promptly after closing so the right owner is billed.

If the house needs repairs, or you hold acreage with a roll-back risk, an as-is cash offer can avoid showings and lender approvals. Any tax or roll-back still comes out of the proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: What is the combined Fauquier County real estate tax rate?
faqs.a: The county's rate page lists $0.895 per $100 of assessed value, made up of $0.709 base, $0.182 fire and rescue and $0.004 conservation easement fund.

faqs.q: When is Fauquier County real estate tax due?
faqs.a: June 5 for the first half and December 5 for the second half, with weekend dates moving to the next business day.

faqs.q: When did Fauquier County last reassess property?
faqs.a: The last reassessment took effect January 1, 2026. New assessed values take effect January 1, 2028.

faqs.q: Who hears assessment appeals in Fauquier County?
faqs.a: The Board of Equalization, a five-member panel appointed by the Circuit Court. Ask the Commissioner of the Revenue for the filing deadline.

faqs.q: Do I owe money back if my Fauquier land is in the use value program?
faqs.a: Possibly. A change from a qualifying use triggers a roll-back, which the county describes as the deferred tax plus 10 percent interest for five years plus the current year.
